claims.text: Crystalline metals and alloys traditionally exhibit a trade-off between strength and ductility.
Multi-objective optimization algorithms can concurrently improve strength and ductility in crystalline metals and alloys.
Concurrent strength–ductility improvement can be achieved by optimizing microstructure.
Concurrent strength–ductility improvement can be achieved by optimizing composition.
The intervention controls grain size and grain-size distribution.
An optimization algorithm can identify a combination of microstructural and compositional parameters that balances strength and ductility.
The optimized material will exhibit a 20% increase in strength relative to traditional alloying and grain-refinement methods.
The optimized material will exhibit a 30% increase in ductility relative to traditional alloying and grain-refinement methods.
The algorithm's predictive and optimization ability is limited by input-data quality.
The algorithm's predictive and optimization ability is limited by microstructural complexity.
The achieved outcome may depend on the specific material system.
The achieved outcome may depend on available computational resources.

contradictions.description: The prediction specifies 20% strength and 30% ductility increases, whereas falsification requires failure to reach only 15% and 25%, respectively. Thus, results below the stated prediction could still pass the falsification rule.
